variants.name: database/sql keyset loop with a base64url token
variants.implementation_notes: Go's standard library offers no pagination helper, so the idiom is a short explicit loop: decode the token, run db.QueryContext(ctx, "SELECT ... WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT $3", ...), walk it with rows.Next()/rows.Scan, fetch page_size + 1 rows to detect the next page, and encode the last row's keys with base64.URLEncoding. Keep the predicate construction in one helper so filter and ordering stay pinned; use google.golang.org/api/iterator only when the collection is behind a Google-style API.
variants.code_sketch:
last := decodeCursor(r.URL.Query().Get("page_token"))
rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx,
    `SELECT id, created_at FROM items
     WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
     ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT $3`,
    last.TS, last.ID, size+1)
if err != nil { return err }
defer rows.Close()
// scan while rows.Next(); cursor = base64.URLEncoding(last row keys); empty at end
pitfalls: rows must be closed before the next query runs on the same *sql.DB: a deferred close inside a pagination loop starves the connection pool once concurrency rises.
Token encoding matters: base64.StdEncoding emits '+' and '/', which corrupt query strings - use base64.URLEncoding, and treat a token echoed back unchanged as an error instead of looping forever.

variants.name: google.golang.org/api/iterator Pager
variants.implementation_notes: For generated Google API clients the iterator package hides the token loop: client iterators expose Next() plus PageInfo() with the next-page Token and the number of items Remaining() on the page, and iterator.NewPager(iterable, pageSize, pageToken).NextPage(&slice) returns control to you with the next token. Reach for it whenever the collection is a Google-style API; keep the hand-written database/sql loop for your own schemas.
pitfalls: iterator.Done is the only end-of-collection signal: treating any other error as the end turns a transient failure into a truncated, successful-looking result.
Capture PageInfo().Token after the last Next() call (or use NewPager/NextPage); reconstructing the next token from the request instead of the response skips or repeats rows.
